title: Put Your Whole Heart Into It
author: Chris Hobbs
summary: Hobbs, writing for Christian school leaders and teachers, argues that the drive to keep improving is a standing part of the educator's vocation, and that it has to be organised rather than left to feeling. He opens with Phil Jackson's remark that he loves total immersion in a pursuit, then roots that drive in the cultural commission and a Thaddeus Williams passage on virtuosity. Excellence, he says, is overused because it is underdefined, and he offers two working definitions: doing a little more than expected, and getting a little better each time. Experience alone guarantees nothing, since a veteran without a humble heart repeats year one many times over. He closes with five practices for a school team: debrief everything, score it, gather end-user feedback, compare your work to something better, and submit to external standards.
points: Excellence is defined as a continuous pursuit of doing a little more than expected and improving a little each time, not as a fixed achievement.
Tenure does not produce growth; a humble, teachable heart does, and without it a 20-year veteran is effectively in year one.
Debrief after every event with a short wins, sins and wonderings review, filed and reopened when the event is planned again.
Measuring, asking the end user, and comparing against someone better are framed as habits that make excellence systematic.
External standards such as degrees, certifications and accreditations are presented as a way to submit one's pursuit of excellence to outside judgment.
quotes: Repetition and experience alone don’t guarantee the pursuit of excellence. A 20-year veteran can still be at year one. How is that possible?
We overuse the word excellence, in my opinion. I’ve actually gone looking for words that are more clearly defined. Maybe that is the real issue: excellence is overused because it is underdefined.
After everything we do, I ask my team to create a document that reviews the “wins, sins, and wonderings.” We file it, then bring it back out when we start planning that event the next year.
The mantra that comparison is the thief of joy. That mantra has given too many of us permission not to learn from the best. Find someone who does what you do better than you do, and learn from them.
Degrees, certifications, fellowships, and accreditations are so valuable here. Submitting to an external standard affirms the pursuit of excellence.

Don tells a great story from his days as a rookie teacher and coach at a school with few resources. Installing a simple scoreboard in a tiny little gym was an act of excellence in that context, and it thrilled the community’s heart.
